tasks.prompt: Milky white water that clears from the bottom up in a glass is reported by many homes in a Manitoba town during a cold snap in January.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional town in a deep cold period. Glass clearing tests and pressure records are available.

evidence.label: A poured glass clears from the bottom upward within a minute, leaving no residue.
The reports spike during the coldest days, when water is near freezing and system pressure is at its winter high.
No breaks, repairs, or flushing occurred in the reporting areas that week.
Samples sent to the laboratory show normal chemistry and no particles.
Neighbouring towns on different supplies report the same milky water during the same cold snap.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by all of the observations?

options.label: White sediment from a failing plant filter is entering the system
Lime is precipitating throughout the distribution system
Cross connections are pulling white chemical into the mains
Tiny air bubbles released from cold, pressurized water are making the water look milky

inference.explanation: Clearing from the bottom up with no residue is the classic behaviour of dissolved air coming out of solution, and the cold snap timing with normal laboratory results supports it. Sediment or lime would leave residue and would not clear upward, and no chemical event is recorded.

nextClue.prompt: Which next check best confirms the explanation and guides the fix?

options.label: Shut down a plant filter for inspection immediately
Show residents the glass test and log whether reports fade as the cold snap eases
Flush the whole system to remove white sediment

nextClue.explanation: The glass test demonstration plus the weather linked pattern confirms harmless air bubbles without disruptive system work.

clueText.nc-a: Filters are passing clear water by laboratory results, so a shutdown is not indicated.
clueText.nc-b: Reports fade as temperatures moderate, and repeated glass tests clear upward with no residue.
clueText.nc-c: Laboratory samples show no particles, so flushing for sediment is not supported.

tasks.prompt: Orange water follows every use of a hydrant for a tanker fill on one rural road in Alberta, affecting the three homes beyond the hydrant for hours.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional rural main with a tanker fill hydrant. Fill logs and complaint times are available.

evidence.label: Complaints begin within an hour of each tanker fill and never occur on days with no fill.
Homes between the plant feed and the hydrant are never affected, only homes beyond it.
Flushing at the end of the road clears the water after each event.
The tanker fills at a high rate that reverses the normal gentle flow in the road main.
On a trial with the fill rate halved, homes beyond the hydrant report no discolouration.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by all of the observations?

options.label: High rate tanker filling stirs up rust deposits in the low flow rural main beyond the hydrant
The tanker is backflowing dirty water into the main
The plant sends orange water whenever a tanker fills
The three homes all have failing services that release rust on fill days

inference.explanation: The timing locked to fills, only downstream homes affected, clearing by flushing, and no event at half fill rate all point to deposits stirred by high fill velocity. Backflow would not be prevented by halving the rate in the same way, and plant water is clear for homes before the hydrant.

nextClue.prompt: Which next check best confirms the explanation and guides the fix?

options.label: Ban all tanker fills permanently
Replace the services of the three homes
Set a maximum fill rate for the tanker station and post it, then track complaints over the next fills

nextClue.explanation: A controlled fill rate tests the velocity explanation in normal operation and protects downstream homes if complaints stop.

clueText.nc-a: Fills are needed for rural supply and the rate trial already shows a workable control.
clueText.nc-b: Services run clear between fills and after flushing, so service failure is not supported.
clueText.nc-c: No discolouration is reported over the next six fills at the posted rate, confirming velocity stirred deposits were the cause.

tasks.prompt: A school in Saskatchewan reports blue green staining on fixtures and a metallic taste, while other buildings on the same street report neither.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional school with copper plumbing, closed for the summer break. Street comparison sampling is available.

evidence.label: First draw samples at the school show elevated copper, and flushed samples after two minutes are near normal.
Street main samples and neighbouring buildings show low copper and no staining complaints.
The school sat closed for eight weeks with water standing in its copper plumbing.
pH of the supplied water is within the normal range for the system and unchanged this year.
Staining is worst at the fixtures farthest from the school service entrance.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by all of the observations?

options.label: A brass valve on the street main is dissolving into the supply
Water standing for weeks in the school copper plumbing over the closure dissolved copper from the pipe walls
The distribution main is delivering high copper water to the street
The plant corrosion control failed this summer

inference.explanation: Street and neighbour samples are low, flushed school samples recover, and the worst fixtures are farthest along the standing plumbing. That pattern is in building stagnation in copper pipe during the closure. A main or plant cause would appear at neighbours and in flushed samples.

nextClue.prompt: Which next check best confirms the explanation and guides the fix?

options.label: Flush the school plumbing thoroughly before reopening and compare first draw copper before and after a normal use week
Replace the street main section feeding the school
Raise the plant corrosion inhibitor dose for the whole system

nextClue.explanation: Pre opening flushing plus a normal use week tests whether regular turnover keeps first draw copper low.

clueText.nc-a: After flushing and a week of normal use, first draw copper is near normal and no new staining appears.
clueText.nc-b: Street samples are already low, so main replacement does not address in building standing water.
clueText.nc-c: System pH and neighbour results are normal, so a system wide dose change is not indicated.

tasks.prompt: Brown water appears across a whole neighbourhood in Alberta for one morning, the morning after the elevated tank was taken out of service and the zone was fed by pumps alone.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional neighbourhood normally fed by gravity from the tank. Tank outage and pump logs are available.

evidence.label: Discolouration is reported across the neighbourhood but not in other zones that morning.
Pump fed operation reversed the normal flow direction in several neighbourhood mains.
Complaints fade by afternoon as the tank returns to service and normal flow direction resumes.
Plant finished water samples that morning are clear with normal iron.
Flushing at two hydrants produces brown water that clears, with rust coloured sediment in the flush discharge.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by all of the observations?

options.label: The drained tank released its sediment into the zone on refill
Groundwater entered the mains while the tank was out
Reversed flow during pump only operation scoured rust deposits from the neighbourhood mains
The plant sent a slug of brown water to the whole town that morning

inference.explanation: Reports are confined to the zone whose flow reversed, plant water is clear, other zones are unaffected, and flushing yields rust sediment. That is scouring from flow reversal. A plant slug would reach other zones, and the tank was out of service, not draining into the zone, during the morning reports.

nextClue.prompt: Which next check best confirms the explanation and guides the fix?

options.label: Excavate to search for groundwater entry points
Flush the reversed sections in the direction of the temporary flow and record which streets clear
Increase plant coagulant dose until complaints stop

nextClue.explanation: Flushing the sections that reversed removes the scoured deposits and maps the affected area for future outage planning.

clueText.nc-a: No breaks or low pressure events occurred to allow groundwater entry.
clueText.nc-b: The reversed sections flush clear and no further complaints follow when normal flow resumes.
clueText.nc-c: Plant finished water was already clear, so a plant dose change does not fit.

tasks.prompt: Rusty water and grit appear at homes near a new subdivision tie in in Manitoba, starting the first week the new main was put into service.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional new main tied into an older street. Commissioning records for the new main are available.

evidence.label: Complaints begin the week the new main enters service and are limited to homes near the tie in.
The new main commissioning record shows flushing was shortened and no final flush to clear was documented.
Water flushed from the tie in hydrant carries sand like grit and construction debris.
Older streets farther from the tie in report no grit at any time.
After a thorough unidirectional flush of the new main, grit complaints stop and do not return.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by all of the observations?

options.label: The old street main suddenly began shedding grit the same week
The plant grit removal failed that week
Home plumbing is generating the grit
Construction debris and dirty water left in the new main at tie in are being carried to nearby homes

inference.explanation: Onset with the new main in service, grit and debris at the tie in flush, no complaints farther away, and a shortened commissioning flush all point to debris left in the new main. The later thorough flush ending complaints confirms it. Older mains and plant causes would not be confined to the tie in area or yield construction debris.

nextClue.prompt: Which next check best confirms the explanation and guides the fix?

options.label: Replace the old street main near the tie in
Advise homes to install whole house grit filters permanently
Complete a full unidirectional flush and swab record for the new main and file the commissioning checklist as incomplete

nextClue.explanation: Completing the flush and documenting the missed commissioning step both fixes the water and prevents a repeat on the next tie in.

clueText.nc-a: Old main water away from the tie in was clear, so replacement is not supported.
clueText.nc-b: Filters would mask a one time debris load that flushing already removes.
clueText.nc-c: The full flush discharges remaining debris, hydrant water runs clear, and no grit is reported in the following month.

tasks.prompt: A faint yellow tint lingers for weeks in a low use cul de sac in a British Columbia town, even though the water entering the cul de sac is clear.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional cul de sac with eight homes and a dead end main. Paired entrance and end sampling is available.

evidence.label: Entrance samples are clear with normal colour and iron on every visit.
End of cul de sac samples show a persistent yellow tint with slightly elevated iron and very low residual.
Several homes are seasonal and vacant for long stretches, so cul de sac demand is very low.
A one time flush clears the tint for only a few days before it slowly returns.
Temperature at the far end is several degrees warmer than at the entrance in summer.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by all of the observations?

options.label: Very low turnover in the cul de sac lets water age, warm, and pick up colour from the main wall between uses
The entrance main delivers tinted water that clears before sampling
One vacant home is backfeeding yellow water into the street
The plant colour removal varies by hour of the day

inference.explanation: Entrance water is clear on every visit while the far end ages, warms, loses residual, and tints again within days of flushing. That is water age in a low demand dead end. Backfeed from one home would not tint flushed hydrant water at the far end, and plant variation would show at the entrance.

nextClue.prompt: Which next check best confirms the explanation and guides the fix?

options.label: Install a timed auto flushing point or loop assessment for the cul de sac and trend end colour weekly
Sample the vacant homes one by one for a month
Raise plant colour removal chemical feed

nextClue.explanation: Regular turnover at the far end directly tests the water age explanation, with weekly colour trending as the measure.

clueText.nc-a: Weekly trending shows colour staying low once regular flushing keeps turnover up at the far end.
clueText.nc-b: Hydrant water at the far end is tinted too, so a single home is not the source.
clueText.nc-c: Entrance samples from the plant supply are already clear.

tasks.prompt: Discoloured water complaints spike town wide in Saskatchewan on the first hot weekend of spring, coinciding with the annual hydrant flushing program start.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional town doing spring unidirectional flushing. Flushing schedule and complaint log are available.

evidence.label: Complaints come almost entirely from streets scheduled for flushing that same day or the day before.
Streets not yet flushed and streets flushed a week earlier report clear water.
Plant finished water is clear throughout the weekend.
Complaint water clears after residents run a cold tap for a few minutes, as the flushing notice advises.
The same pattern occurred on the same program weekend the previous spring.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by all of the observations?

options.label: Source water turned over in the reservoir that weekend
Planned flushing velocities are stirring deposits in the mains being flushed, causing temporary discolouration nearby
A plant process upset is sending dirty water town wide
A major main break is stirring the whole system

inference.explanation: Complaints track the flushing schedule street by street, plant water is clear, water clears with a short tap run, and the pattern repeats each program spring. That is expected flushing disturbance. A plant upset or break would not follow the street schedule or spare unflushed streets.

nextClue.prompt: Which next check best confirms the explanation and guides the fix?

options.label: Double the plant coagulant dose for the weekend
Continue the program with advance notices and log complaints by street against the flushing schedule
Cancel the flushing program for the year

nextClue.explanation: Logging complaints against the schedule confirms the link and improves notice timing for the remaining streets.

clueText.nc-a: Plant water is clear, so a plant dose change does not fit the street pattern.
clueText.nc-b: Complaints continue to match only the streets being flushed and stop town wide when the program ends.
clueText.nc-c: Cancelling would leave deposits and dead end quality problems unaddressed.

tasks.prompt: Dark brown water with a musty odour comes from one hydrant in Alberta during testing, while taps at nearby homes are clear and odour free.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional hydrant on a short stub main that is rarely used. Home comparison sampling is available.

evidence.label: The hydrant stub main serves no homes and is opened only for testing once or twice a year.
Water from the hydrant clears after several minutes of flushing and the odour fades with it.
Nearby home taps are clear before, during, and after the hydrant test.
Residual in the hydrant stub sample is near zero, while home samples are normal.
The main feeding the stub shows normal residual and clarity at the junction.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by all of the observations?

options.label: The plant sent musty water to the neighbourhood that day
The hydrant barrel is contaminated with soil
Water standing in the rarely used hydrant stub has aged, lost residual, and picked up colour and odour in the stub
The whole street main has the same dark water

inference.explanation: Home taps and the junction main are normal while only the isolated stub is dark, aged, and residual free, and it clears with flushing. That is stub stagnation, not a street or plant cause. Soil contamination would not explain the near zero residual pattern matching age.

nextClue.prompt: Which next check best confirms the explanation and guides the fix?

options.label: Flush the entire street main system for a day
Take the hydrant out of service permanently
Flush the stub to clear before testing and add the stub to the dead end flushing list

nextClue.explanation: Adding the stub to routine flushing keeps its water turned over and verifies home quality stays normal.

clueText.nc-a: Street main samples at the junction were already normal.
clueText.nc-b: The hydrant is needed for fire protection and works normally once the stub is flushed.
clueText.nc-c: The stub flushes clear quickly on the routine list and test water is acceptable thereafter.

tasks.prompt: White flakes that do not dissolve appear in water at homes in a new Manitoba subdivision, while the town older sections report none.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional new subdivision with plastic mains. Flake samples were collected for simple checks.

evidence.label: The flakes are hard, white, and gritty, and are identified as plastic shavings and joint compound residue.
Complaints are limited to the newest phase, where main and service construction finished last month.
Flushing at phase hydrants discharges more flakes at first, then runs clear.
Older phases of the same subdivision, built two years earlier, report no flakes.
Plant and reservoir samples contain no flakes.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by all of the observations?

options.label: The plant is precipitating white mineral flakes into all water
The reservoir lining is flaking into the supply
Home softeners are shedding white resin beads at every home
Construction residue left in the newest phase mains and services is washing out to homes

inference.explanation: Flakes identified as plastic shavings and joint residue, limited to the newest phase, discharging during hydrant flushing, and absent at the plant and older phases point to construction residue. A plant or reservoir cause would reach older sections, and softener beads would not appear at hydrants.

nextClue.prompt: Which next check best confirms the explanation and guides the fix?

options.label: Flush the newest phase mains thoroughly and inspect a service sample after flushing
Soften the plant water further to stop mineral flakes
Relign the reservoir

nextClue.explanation: Thorough phase flushing removes the residue, and a clear service sample confirms homes should stop seeing flakes.

clueText.nc-a: Phase hydrants run clear after flushing and flake reports stop within a week.
clueText.nc-b: The flakes are plastic and compound, not mineral, so softening does not fit.
clueText.nc-c: Reservoir samples contain no flakes.

tasks.prompt: Green water is reported from taps in one older building in a British Columbia town after a plumbing renovation, with no complaints elsewhere in the system.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional older building with new copper plumbing installed during renovation. System sampling is available.

evidence.label: System samples across town, including the street at the building, show normal copper and clear water.
Building samples show elevated copper, worst in first draw morning samples.
The renovation installed long runs of new copper pipe in the building.
Flushed building samples after several minutes are near normal for copper.
No other building on the street reports green water or staining.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by all of the observations?

options.label: New copper plumbing in the building is releasing copper into standing water until the pipe surfaces condition with use
The town supply has become corrosive to copper everywhere this month
The street main is made of copper and is dissolving
A chemical spill entered the main at the building

inference.explanation: Only this building is affected, street and town samples are normal, and first draw samples are worst after standing in new copper runs. That is new pipe copper release inside the building. A town wide corrosive change would affect other buildings, and the street main is not copper.

nextClue.prompt: Which next check best confirms the explanation and guides the fix?

options.label: Excavate and replace the street main
Flush the building system and advise running taps before use until first draw copper trends down over several weeks
Change the town corrosion control program immediately

nextClue.explanation: Trending first draw copper while the new pipe conditions tests whether levels fall with normal use and flushing.

clueText.nc-a: The main is not copper and its water tests normal.
clueText.nc-b: First draw copper falls steadily over three weeks and the green tint disappears.
clueText.nc-c: Town and street samples are normal, so a system program change is not supported.

tasks.prompt: Cloudy brown water appears only when a specific fire hall hydrant in Saskatchewan is flow tested each year, alarming the two nearest homes.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional hydrant on a dead end spur serving the fire hall. Annual test records are available.

evidence.label: Cloudiness at the two homes begins during the annual hydrant flow test and clears within hours afterward.
The spur main beyond the homes to the hydrant is a dead end that carries almost no daily flow.
Homes on the looped street before the spur are unaffected during the test.
Flushing the spur a week before the test, in a trial, results in no complaints during that year test.
Residual at the end of the spur is low before flushing and normal after.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by all of the observations?

options.label: The plant cannot keep up during the test and sends dirty water
The high test flow scours aged deposits from the low flow dead end spur serving the hydrant
The hydrant itself is rusting internally and colours the whole system
Fire hall plumbing backflows into the homes

inference.explanation: Effects are limited to homes on the dead end spur, begin and end with the test, and are prevented by pre flushing the spur. That is scouring of spur deposits by test flow. A hydrant or plant cause would affect the looped street too, and backflow from one building would not be prevented by spur flushing.

nextClue.prompt: Which next check best confirms the explanation and guides the fix?

options.label: Cancel annual hydrant flow testing
Replace the fire hall plumbing
Schedule spur flushing a week before each annual hydrant test and notify the two homes

nextClue.explanation: Pre test flushing is the direct control if scouring is the cause, and the trial already supports it, so confirming it as routine practice is the check.

clueText.nc-a: Testing is required for fire protection readiness and the spur flush already controls the problem.
clueText.nc-b: Flushed spur water carries the deposits, so hall plumbing is not the source.
clueText.nc-c: With routine pre flushing, the next annual test produces clear water and no complaints.

tasks.prompt: Free chlorine holds at 0.9 mg/L leaving a plant in Alberta and at mid system taps, but streets beyond a ground level reservoir read 0.1 mg/L or less.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional system with a ground level reservoir between the plant and the affected streets. Reservoir level and sampling records are available.

evidence.label: Samples at the reservoir inlet read 0.85 mg/L while samples at its outlet read 0.15 mg/L on the same day.
The reservoir level cycles only between 85 and 95 percent full, so most of its volume sits for many days.
Reservoir water temperature is 24 C and a sediment layer is visible through the inspection hatch.
Streets fed directly from the plant, bypassing the reservoir, hold 0.8 mg/L.
A trial that lowers the operating band and cycles the reservoir deeply raises outlet residual to 0.5 mg/L within days.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by all of the observations?

options.label: The affected streets have a large leak diluting the residual
The outlet sampling tap is contaminated and reads falsely low
The reservoir stores water so long, warm and over sediment, that residual is consumed before the water leaves
The plant chlorine dose has been cut without the operators knowing

inference.explanation: Residual falls across the reservoir itself, from 0.85 to 0.15 mg/L, while direct fed streets hold 0.8 mg/L on the same plant dose. Shallow level cycling, warm water, sediment, and recovery under deep cycling all point to storage decay. A leak cannot remove chlorine selectively, and a faulty tap cannot explain the trial recovery.

nextClue.prompt: Which next check best confirms the explanation and guides the fix?

options.label: Set a deeper reservoir cycling range and schedule an interior cleaning inspection, then trend outlet residual daily
Double the plant chlorine dose for the whole system
Replace the reservoir outlet sampling tap and wait a month

nextClue.explanation: Deep cycling plus a cleaning inspection attacks the storage decay directly, and daily outlet trending verifies whether residual recovers and holds.

clueText.nc-a: Outlet residual climbs to 0.55 mg/L and holds for two weeks under deep cycling, confirming storage age and sediment demand were the cause.
clueText.nc-b: Doubling the plant dose would over chlorinate the direct fed streets that already hold 0.8 mg/L.
clueText.nc-c: The tap agreed with a second flushed sample, so replacing it does not test storage decay.

tasks.prompt: Chlorine residual is normal entering one street in Saskatchewan but nearly gone 400 m later, and the loss has grown worse over two summers.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional street on an old unlined cast iron main. Paired sampling points bracket the street.

evidence.label: Paired same day samples read 0.8 mg/L at the street entrance and 0.1 mg/L at the far hydrant.
The street main is unlined cast iron with heavy internal rust tubercles confirmed on a repair coupon.
Flushing the street restores far end residual for about two days, then it decays again.
A parallel street on a newer lined main, with the same water age, holds 0.6 mg/L at its far end.
Iron in far end samples is elevated and the water there is slightly yellow after standing overnight.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by all of the observations?

options.label: Water age alone explains the loss, since the lined street loses residual the same way
The far hydrant sample tap leaks and dilutes the sample
The plant dose falls every afternoon when the street is sampled
The rough rusted interior of the old main exerts a high chlorine demand that consumes residual along the street

inference.explanation: The lined street with the same water age holds its residual, which rules out age alone. Heavy tuberculation on a repair coupon, elevated iron, and only two days of relief after flushing show the pipe wall demand consuming chlorine. A leaking sample tap would not raise iron or follow the flushing pattern.

nextClue.prompt: Which next check best confirms the explanation and guides the fix?

options.label: Move the far sampling point to the street entrance
Sample residual at several points along the street before and after a cleaning trial on one section
Raise the plant dose until the far end reads normal

nextClue.explanation: Point by point sampling around a cleaned section directly tests whether wall demand falls where deposits are removed.

clueText.nc-a: Moving the sample point would hide the far end loss instead of testing it.
clueText.nc-b: Residual holds much farther along the cleaned section than the uncleaned section at the same water age.
clueText.nc-c: Raising the plant dose would over chlorinate the rest of the system for one street wall demand problem.

tasks.prompt: Residual disappears at the far end of a long dead end in Manitoba every August, while the rest of the system holds normal residual all summer.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional long dead end serving six homes. Monthly sampling and temperature records are available.

evidence.label: Far end residual is 0.6 mg/L in May, 0.3 mg/L in July, and undetectable in August, while system samples stay near 0.7 mg/L.
Far end water temperature rises from 10 C in May to 22 C in August.
Demand on the dead end is very low, with some homes vacant for weeks in summer.
Flushing in August restores far end residual to 0.6 mg/L, but it falls again within two weeks.
A looped street of the same length nearby holds residual through August.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by all of the observations?

options.label: Warm temperature plus very long water age at the low demand dead end consumes the residual each August
The plant stops chlorinating every August
A seasonal cross connection dilutes the dead end each summer
The August samples are all taken with expired reagents

inference.explanation: The seasonal fall tracks temperature and age at this dead end only, system samples stay normal, the looped comparison street holds residual, and flushing gives only temporary relief. That is age and warmth driven decay. A plant stop would affect the whole system, and expired reagents would not follow the flushing relief pattern.

nextClue.prompt: Which next check best confirms the explanation and guides the fix?

options.label: Order new sample reagents and repeat August sampling next year
Raise the whole system dose for the month of August
Put the dead end on an August auto flushing schedule and trend residual weekly through the month

nextClue.explanation: Weekly trending under scheduled flushing tests whether added turnover holds residual through the warm period.

clueText.nc-a: Reagents were verified in date and system samples read normally with the same kits.
clueText.nc-b: System residual is already normal, so a system wide increase is not targeted.
clueText.nc-c: Far end residual holds above 0.4 mg/L through August under scheduled flushing.

tasks.prompt: A booster chlorination station in a British Columbia system shows normal dose records, yet residual downstream has fallen steadily for a month.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional booster station feeding a distant zone. Dose, tank, and downstream sampling records are available.

evidence.label: Booster chemical tank level falls at the normal rate and the feed pump runs on schedule.
Downstream residual has fallen from 0.7 to 0.2 mg/L over a month while plant residual is unchanged.
A sample drawn directly from the booster discharge reads near zero chlorine.
The chemical in the tank is found to be a year old, stored through a hot summer in a sunlit room, and much weaker than its label strength.
A trial feed from a fresh chemical tote restores booster discharge residual the same day.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by all of the observations?

options.label: Downstream sampling points have all moved farther away
The aged, heat weakened chemical in the booster tank is feeding at normal volume but at a fraction of its expected strength
The downstream zone demand for chlorine suddenly tripled
The feed pump has stopped working

inference.explanation: Feed volume and pump operation are normal, yet discharge residual is near zero, the chemical is old and heat degraded, and fresh chemical restores residual the same day. That is strength loss, not volume loss or a demand change. A demand tripling would not leave discharge residual near zero at the station outlet.

nextClue.prompt: Which next check best confirms the explanation and guides the fix?

options.label: Test the stored chemical strength, replace it with fresh stock, and set a storage age and temperature limit
Increase the feed pump rate to three times normal
Move downstream sampling points closer to the station

nextClue.explanation: Strength testing plus fresh stock directly confirms the degradation explanation and sets a prevention limit.

clueText.nc-a: Stored chemical tests at a third of label strength, fresh stock restores downstream residual within two days, and a storage limit is set.
clueText.nc-b: Tripling the rate with weak chemical wastes chemical and does not confirm the strength loss.
clueText.nc-c: Moving sample points would hide the zone loss instead of fixing it.

tasks.prompt: Residual is strong on weekdays but fades every weekend in a small industrial area in Alberta where the plant that uses most water shuts down on Fridays.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional industrial branch main with one dominant customer. Flow and residual records by day are available.

evidence.label: Weekday residual on the branch is 0.7 mg/L and weekend residual falls to 0.1 mg/L by Sunday night.
Branch flow drops to near zero from Friday evening to Monday morning.
Monday morning flushing restores residual, and the first water drawn has a stale taste.
Residential streets on the same feed hold normal residual through weekends.
Water temperature in the branch rises over each still weekend in summer.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by all of the observations?

options.label: Weekend staff sample with a different, faulty meter
The industrial customer backflows chlorine free water into the branch on weekends
Weekend stagnation in the branch main while the main customer is shut down lets residual decay before Monday
The treatment plant reduces its dose on weekends

inference.explanation: The day pattern follows branch flow exactly, residential streets on the same feed stay normal, and Monday flushing restores residual. That is weekend stagnation in the branch. A plant dose cut would affect the residential streets too, and a meter fault would not produce stale taste in the first Monday water.

nextClue.prompt: Which next check best confirms the explanation and guides the fix?

options.label: Replace the weekend sampling meter
Program a small weekend flush or bleed at the branch end and trend Sunday night residual
Ask the plant to raise the weekend dose for the whole system

nextClue.explanation: A weekend turnover measure tests the stagnation explanation at the branch itself, tracked by Sunday sampling.

clueText.nc-a: Weekday and weekend meters were compared and agree on split samples.
clueText.nc-b: Sunday night residual holds above 0.4 mg/L once weekend flushing keeps the branch turning over.
clueText.nc-c: The rest of the system holds normal weekend residual, so a system dose change is not needed.

tasks.prompt: Two elevated tanks serve one zone in Saskatchewan. Streets below one tank hold residual, while streets below the other read low, though both tanks receive the same water.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional zone with two elevated tanks of different ages and use. Tank level records are available.

evidence.label: Tank A cycles through most of its volume daily and its downstream streets hold 0.6 mg/L.
Tank B level barely moves, staying near full for weeks, and its downstream streets read 0.1 mg/L.
Inlet residual to both tanks is the same at 0.8 mg/L.
Tank B serves a new area where most lots are still vacant, so its demand is very low.
A trial that draws Tank B down daily for a week raises its downstream residual to 0.45 mg/L.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by all of the observations?

options.label: Tank B has a leak that lets untreated groundwater in
The plant sends different water to the two tanks
Tank B downstream samples are taken from a dead sampling line
Tank B water sits nearly still because its service area demand is very low, so residual decays in storage

inference.explanation: Both tanks receive the same 0.8 mg/L water, Tank A cycles and holds residual, Tank B barely moves and does not, and drawing Tank B down restores residual in a trial. That is storage age from low turnover. Groundwater entry would need a pressure loss that is not observed, and a dead sample line would not respond to tank drawdown.

nextClue.prompt: Which next check best confirms the explanation and guides the fix?

options.label: Raise the plant dose until Tank B streets read normal
Replace the Tank B downstream sampling line
Set Tank B to a daily drawdown and refill cycle and trend downstream residual for two weeks

nextClue.explanation: A controlled cycling regime tests turnover directly, and trending shows whether residual recovers and holds.

clueText.nc-a: Raising the plant dose would push Tank A streets well above target for a Tank B turnover problem.
clueText.nc-b: A flushed second sample at the same point agreed with the first, so the line is not dead.
clueText.nc-c: Downstream residual holds near 0.5 mg/L under daily cycling of Tank B.

tasks.prompt: Residual drops sharply across a short section of new plastic main in Manitoba, while older sections before and after it hold normal residual.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional new plastic section installed during a renewal last month. Section sampling is available.

evidence.label: Samples before the new section read 0.75 mg/L and after it read 0.2 mg/L on the same day.
The new section was pressure tested, then sat full of untreated test water for three weeks before being tied in.
Commissioning records show the section was not flushed or disinfected after the long standing period.
Sections farther downstream recover gradually to 0.5 mg/L.
After a thorough flush and disinfection of the new section, samples across it read 0.7 mg/L.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by all of the observations?

options.label: Untreated water standing for weeks in the new section consumed residual and seeded demand that the flow now meets at the tie in
New plastic pipe always destroys chlorine permanently
The plant dose fell during the month the section was installed
A valve is bypassing treated water around the section

inference.explanation: Residual falls only across the section that stood full of untreated water without flushing or disinfection, and recovers after the section is flushed and disinfected. That is a commissioning gap, not a plastic property, since other plastic sections in town hold residual. A plant dose fall would show before the section too.

nextClue.prompt: Which next check best confirms the explanation and guides the fix?

options.label: Review the commissioning record, flush and disinfect the section to standard, and resample across it
Replace the new plastic section with ductile iron
Raise the plant dose for a month

nextClue.explanation: Completing the missed commissioning steps and resampling is the direct confirmation and fix.

clueText.nc-a: After proper flushing and disinfection, residual across the section holds at 0.7 mg/L for two weeks.
clueText.nc-b: Other plastic sections hold residual normally, so the material is not the cause.
clueText.nc-c: Plant and upstream samples are normal, so a dose increase is not indicated.

tasks.prompt: A rural hamlet in Alberta on a long supply main reports residual fading in the afternoon and recovering overnight, every day in summer.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional hamlet at the end of a 12 km supply main. Hourly residual and flow logging is available.

evidence.label: Residual at the hamlet is 0.6 mg/L at 06:00, falls to 0.15 mg/L by 16:00, and recovers overnight.
Daytime flow in the supply main is high for irrigation, so water arriving in the afternoon left the plant at midday in peak heat.
Overnight arriving water travelled slowly and arrived in the cool early hours, but with the same travel time pattern reversed in logging.
Main water temperature at the hamlet peaks in the late afternoon.
On a cloudy, cool week the afternoon fade is much smaller at the same flows.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by all of the observations?

options.label: The hamlet sampling tap is in direct sun and heats the samples
Warm afternoon water temperature in the long main speeds residual decay for water arriving later in the day
The plant doses less chlorine in the afternoon
Hamlet residents use a chemical that removes chlorine each afternoon

inference.explanation: The daily cycle tracks water temperature and travel, shrinks in cool cloudy weather, and occurs at the hamlet only. That is temperature driven decay along a long main. A plant dose pattern would show at other points on the main, and a sun heated tap would not follow cloudy week behaviour of flushed samples.

nextClue.prompt: Which next check best confirms the explanation and guides the fix?

options.label: Replace the hamlet sampling tap with a shaded model
Log residual and temperature together at two points along the main for a hot week
Ask the plant to dose only in the morning

nextClue.explanation: Paired point logging shows where along the main the afternoon decay grows, which guides any booster or shading decision.

clueText.nc-a: Flushed samples drawn to a shaded bottle show the same afternoon fade.
clueText.nc-b: Logging shows decay accelerating in the warmest downstream half of the main on hot afternoons.
clueText.nc-c: Plant dose records are steady through the day.

tasks.prompt: Residual at a recreation centre in a British Columbia town is repeatedly low, while the street hydrant outside reads normal on the same days.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional recreation centre with a long internal service and a storage tank for its pool systems. Paired sampling is available.

evidence.label: Hydrant samples outside read 0.7 mg/L while centre tap samples read 0.15 mg/L on the same mornings.
The centre service passes through a large internal storage tank that turns over slowly.
Centre samples drawn after the tank is bypassed in a trial read 0.65 mg/L.
The centre was closed for two weeks before the low readings began, with water standing in its systems.
Street samples on both sides of the centre are normal.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by all of the observations?

options.label: The centre sampling staff use an incorrect test method
The pool chemicals are entering the drinking taps and removing chlorine
Water ageing in the centre internal storage tank and standing plumbing consumes residual before the taps
The street main residual collapses at the centre service only

inference.explanation: Street and hydrant water is normal, bypassing the internal tank restores tap residual, and the closure left water standing in the building systems. That localizes decay inside the centre. A street cause would show at the hydrant, and the trial bypass result rules out a pure testing error.

nextClue.prompt: Which next check best confirms the explanation and guides the fix?

options.label: Flush the street main serving the centre
Retrain sampling staff and take no other action
Flush the centre systems, set the internal tank to cycle daily, and resample taps after a week of normal use

nextClue.explanation: Restoring turnover inside the building and resampling tests the internal ageing explanation directly.

clueText.nc-a: Street hydrant water was already normal, so street flushing does not address the building tank.
clueText.nc-b: Split samples by utility staff agreed with centre results, so method is not the cause.
clueText.nc-c: Tap residual recovers to 0.6 mg/L after flushing and daily tank cycling.

tasks.prompt: Chlorine residual across a whole small town in Saskatchewan falls over three days during a heat wave, even though the plant dose is unchanged.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional small town with one reservoir and short mains. Plant, reservoir, and town sampling records are available.

evidence.label: Plant finished water holds 0.9 mg/L through the heat wave.
Reservoir outlet falls from 0.7 to 0.3 mg/L over three hot days, and town taps fall with it.
Reservoir water temperature rises to 26 C and the reservoir is at its summer high level with slow turnover.
Algae growth is visible on the reservoir water surface near the hatch in inspection photos.
Shading and deeper cycling in a trial over the next hot spell holds outlet residual near 0.6 mg/L.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by all of the observations?

options.label: Every main in town developed a leak during the heat wave
The plant analyzer is reading high and the true dose has fallen
Residents are all using more chlorine removing filters that week
Heat, high stored volume, slow turnover, and algae demand in the reservoir are consuming residual town wide

inference.explanation: Plant water is steady, the fall occurs across the reservoir, and it tracks heat, high level, slow turnover, and algae, with recovery under deeper cycling in the next hot spell. That is reservoir decay at system scale. Leaks do not remove chlorine town wide in this pattern, and a faulty analyzer would not be corrected by cycling.

nextClue.prompt: Which next check best confirms the explanation and guides the fix?

options.label: Set a heat wave reservoir cycling and inspection routine and trend outlet residual daily during hot spells
Replace all town mains showing age
Recalibrate the plant analyzer and take no other action

nextClue.explanation: A heat routine aimed at the reservoir tests the storage decay explanation where the fall is measured.

clueText.nc-a: Outlet residual holds near 0.6 mg/L through the next hot spell under the cycling and inspection routine.
clueText.nc-b: Town mains show no new leak losses in flow records.
clueText.nc-c: The analyzer was verified against grab samples and reads correctly.

tasks.prompt: A dead end in Manitoba tests positive for low residual and stale taste each spring after snowmelt, then improves on its own by early summer.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional dead end near a low lying area. Spring sampling and winter records are available.

evidence.label: Spring far end residual is near zero with stale taste, while the dead end entrance is normal.
Winter records show the dead end bleeder was closed all winter to save water, so the end section barely turned over for months.
Neighbouring dead ends with bleeders left running hold spring residual.
Flushing restores the end within a day each spring.
No breaks or flooding of the main occurred over the winter.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by all of the observations?

options.label: Months of near zero turnover over winter, with the bleeder closed, left the end section aged and residual free by spring
Snowmelt water entered the main and diluted the residual
The plant dose is cut every winter
Spring sampling is done by new staff who make errors

inference.explanation: Entrance water is normal, neighbouring dead ends with running bleeders are fine, the bleeder here was closed all winter, and flushing restores quality in a day. That is winter stagnation from the closed bleeder. Snowmelt entry would need a break or flooding, neither of which occurred.

nextClue.prompt: Which next check best confirms the explanation and guides the fix?

options.label: Raise the plant winter dose for the whole town
Restore the winter bleeder or a scheduled winter flushing for this dead end and sample at spring melt
Wait for early summer improvement and take no action

nextClue.explanation: Restoring winter turnover tests the stagnation explanation through the next winter and spring.

clueText.nc-a: Town and entrance residuals are normal, so a town wide dose change is not targeted.
clueText.nc-b: The following spring, far end residual is normal after a winter of scheduled turnover.
clueText.nc-c: Waiting leaves the stale, residual free water in place each spring.

tasks.prompt: Residual is normal at a tank outlet in Alberta but low at the first streets below the tank, only on mornings after the tank sits idle overnight.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional elevated tank with a single inlet outlet pipe. Morning sampling at tank and streets is available.

evidence.label: Tank outlet samples drawn from the tank tap read 0.7 mg/L in the morning.
First street samples read 0.2 mg/L on mornings after idle nights, and 0.6 mg/L on mornings after the tank cycled overnight.
The tank inlet outlet pipe run between the tank and the first streets is long and holds a large volume.
Water standing in that pipe run overnight is the first water delivered to the streets in the morning.
Flushing the pipe run in a trial before morning sampling gives street samples of 0.65 mg/L.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by all of the observations?

options.label: Morning sampling staff rush and test poorly
Water standing overnight in the long inlet outlet pipe run loses residual before it reaches the first streets
The tank water itself loses residual every night
The first streets have a morning cross connection

inference.explanation: Tank tap water is normal, streets are low only after idle nights, and flushing the pipe run restores street samples. That isolates the overnight loss to the standing pipe run, not the tank. A cross connection would not be cured by flushing the run, and rushed testing would not follow the cycling pattern.

nextClue.prompt: Which next check best confirms the explanation and guides the fix?

options.label: Raise the tank outlet target residual for the whole zone
Replace the first street sampling taps
Program a small overnight circulation or morning flush of the pipe run and trend first street residual

nextClue.explanation: Adding turnover to the pipe run tests the standing water explanation at the exact section where the loss occurs.

clueText.nc-a: Tank water is already normal, so raising its target does not address the pipe run.
clueText.nc-b: Flushed duplicate samples agreed, so the taps are not the problem.
clueText.nc-c: First street morning residual holds normal once the pipe run is kept turning over overnight.

tasks.prompt: Free chlorine residual fades fastest in the oldest part of a town in Alberta, street by street, in order of pipe age.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional town where pipe age varies by neighbourhood. Age mapped sampling is available. This system uses free chlorine.

evidence.label: Streets with 70 year old unlined mains average 0.15 mg/L at their far ends.
Streets with 30 year old lined mains average 0.5 mg/L at the same water age.
New plastic streets average 0.7 mg/L at the same water age.
Entrance residual is the same 0.85 mg/L for all three areas.
Cleaning and lining a trial old street raises its far end average to 0.5 mg/L the following season.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by all of the observations?

options.label: The plant dose is lower when it supplies the old town
Sampling teams spend longer reaching old town samples
Older unlined pipe wall demand, increasing with pipe age and roughness, consumes residual street by street
Water age is longer in the old part of town than everywhere else

inference.explanation: Entrance residual and water age are matched across areas, yet far end residual falls in exact pipe age order, and lining a trial street restores it. That is wall demand tied to pipe condition. Age of water and dose are controlled in the comparison, and sample holding was the same for all areas.

nextClue.prompt: Which next check best confirms the explanation and guides the fix?

options.label: Prioritize the oldest unlined streets for cleaning and lining assessment using the age mapped residual results
Raise the plant dose until the oldest streets read normal
Resample old town with a faster delivery route

nextClue.explanation: The age mapped results directly support a condition based renewal priority, verified by the trial street recovery.

clueText.nc-a: The trial street holds its recovered residual for a full season after lining, supporting the renewal priority.
clueText.nc-b: A dose high enough for the oldest walls would over chlorinate new streets that already read 0.7 mg/L.
clueText.nc-c: Split samples delivered by both routes agreed, so delivery time is not the cause.

tasks.prompt: Residual at a hospital service in Saskatchewan reads low on the utility side sample, alarming staff, but repeat sampling with a fully flushed tap reads normal.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional hospital with a dedicated sampling tap on its service. Sampling procedure review is available.

evidence.label: The first low sample was drawn from a little used tap without flushing, first thing Monday after a quiet weekend.
A fully flushed sample at the same tap, drawn minutes later, reads 0.7 mg/L.
Street hydrant samples beside the hospital read 0.7 mg/L on both days.
The service line to the sampling tap is long and the tap is used only for weekly sampling.
Flushed samples taken on three following days all read normal.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by all of the observations?

options.label: The street supply residual collapses every Monday
The hospital service main is failing and consuming chlorine
The laboratory misread the first sample
The unflushed sample represented water that stood in the long service and tap line over the weekend, not the street supply

inference.explanation: Hydrant water is normal, a flushed sample minutes later is normal, and flushed samples stay normal for days. The first sample came from an unflushed, little used tap after a quiet weekend, so it measured standing line water. A street or service main failure would not clear with a short flush and stay normal.

nextClue.prompt: Which next check best confirms the explanation and guides the fix?

options.label: Ask the laboratory to discard the low result as an error
Set a flushed sampling procedure for the service tap and record flush time with each result
Excavate and replace the hospital service main

nextClue.explanation: A documented flush procedure tests whether all future samples at this tap represent the supply, which is the actual weakness found.

clueText.nc-a: Discarding the result without fixing the procedure would leave the same trap in place.
clueText.nc-b: Weekly samples under the flushed procedure read normal for a month, with flush times recorded.
clueText.nc-c: Flushed and hydrant samples are normal, so main replacement is not supported.

tasks.prompt: After a reservoir cleaning in Manitoba, residual downstream is excellent for a month, then fades faster than before the cleaning over the next season.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional reservoir returned to service after cleaning. Post cleaning sampling trend is available.

evidence.label: Outlet residual is 0.8 mg/L for a month after cleaning, then declines month by month to 0.2 mg/L.
Inspection at the end of the season finds a heavy sediment layer rebuilt and a failed inlet baffle that short circuits flow across the reservoir.
Level records show the same shallow cycling as before cleaning.
Streets bypassing the reservoir hold normal residual all season.
Repairing the baffle and deepening cycling in a trial holds outlet residual the next season.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by all of the observations?

options.label: A failed inlet baffle short circuits the reservoir, so most water ages over rebuilt sediment and loses residual
The cleaning crew contaminated the reservoir permanently
The plant dose declined steadily all season
Downstream mains aged a full season in a few months

inference.explanation: Initial recovery after cleaning, then a steady fade with a rebuilt sediment layer, a failed baffle causing short circuiting, and recovery when the baffle is repaired and cycling deepened all point to reservoir hydraulics and sediment demand returning. Plant dose is steady and bypass streets are normal, ruling out a plant cause.

nextClue.prompt: Which next check best confirms the explanation and guides the fix?

options.label: Clean the reservoir again every month
Raise the plant dose each month to match the fade
Repair the inlet baffle, set deep cycling, and schedule sediment checks with outlet residual trending

nextClue.explanation: Repairing the flow path and trending residual tests whether short circuiting was the driver of the renewed fade.

clueText.nc-a: Monthly cleaning is disruptive and the baffle fault would still short circuit the flow.
clueText.nc-b: Bypass streets already hold normal residual on the current dose.
clueText.nc-c: Outlet residual holds near target through the next season after baffle repair and deep cycling.

tasks.prompt: Night flows in a district metered area in Alberta stay high all winter, while daytime flows match the same months last year.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional district with a metered inlet and logged flows. Customer use is mostly residential.

evidence.label: Minimum night flow between 02:00 and 04:00 is double last winter at the same time.
Daytime and evening flows match last year closely.
No new large customers connected in the district this year.
Acoustic listening on one street finds a strong leak noise at a hydrant branch valve.
When that branch is isolated for one night in a trial, district night flow falls to last winter level.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by all of the observations?

options.label: A new industrial night shift customer is using the extra water
A continuous leak on the hydrant branch is running day and night and shows up most clearly in the minimum night flow
Residents have doubled their overnight water use this winter
The district inlet meter has drifted high on all flows

inference.explanation: A leak runs continuously, so it dominates the quiet night flow while barely changing busy daytime flow, and isolating the noisy branch returns night flow to normal for a night. A meter drift would raise daytime readings too, and no new customer or use change is recorded.

nextClue.prompt: Which next check best confirms the explanation and guides the fix?

options.label: Excavate the noisy hydrant branch, repair the leak found, and log night flow for the following week
Replace the district inlet meter
Survey residents about overnight water use

nextClue.explanation: Repair followed by night flow logging is the direct proof that the leak accounted for the excess night flow.

clueText.nc-a: Night flow stays at last winter level for a week after the branch joint leak is repaired.
clueText.nc-b: Daytime accuracy checks show the inlet meter reads correctly.
clueText.nc-c: The isolation trial already located the loss without a survey.

tasks.prompt: A wet patch and green grass strip persist over a main in a Manitoba town through a dry August, with no rain for three weeks.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional 200 mm main under a grass boulevard. Weather and repair records are available.

evidence.label: The wet patch sits directly over the main alignment and grows slowly week by week.
Soil in the patch is saturated even though surrounding boulevard soil is dry and cracked.
Water sampled from the patch excavation test hole contains chlorine residual matching the distribution water.
No irrigation system serves that boulevard section.
Acoustic logging peaks in leak noise at the centre of the wet patch.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by all of the observations?

options.label: Storm drain water is leaking upward into the boulevard
Residents are dumping water on the patch nightly
A leak from the main is saturating the soil above it and keeping the patch wet through the dry spell
A natural spring has broken through under the boulevard

inference.explanation: Chlorinated water in the test hole, saturation confined over the main during a drought, and peak leak noise at the patch centre together identify a main leak. A spring or storm water would not carry distribution chlorine residual, and nightly dumping would not produce the acoustic peak.

nextClue.prompt: Which next check best confirms the explanation and guides the fix?

options.label: Wait for autumn rain to see if the patch changes
Excavate at the acoustic peak and repair the main, then confirm the patch dries over the following weeks
Install a drain to carry the spring water away

nextClue.explanation: Excavation at the noise peak is the direct confirmation and the repair location.

clueText.nc-a: Waiting leaves treated water leaking and the soil saturated.
clueText.nc-b: A cracked joint is found at the peak location, and after repair the patch dries within two weeks.
clueText.nc-c: The water carries chlorine residual, so it is treated supply, not spring water.

tasks.prompt: One home in Saskatchewan reports a hissing sound at its service line at night and a water bill three times normal, with no visible water inside the home.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional home with a meter inside. Night listening and meter checks are available.

evidence.label: The home meter dial moves steadily when all taps and appliances are confirmed off.
Closing the curb stop stops the meter movement and the hissing sound.
No water is visible in the basement, yard, or driveway.
A listening device on the service traces the strongest noise midway between the curb and the home, under the lawn.
Neighbour meters on the same street show normal use.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by all of the observations?

options.label: The meter is over registering and the hissing is a faulty tap washer
A toilet is running continuously inside the home
The street main is leaking under the lawn
The home service line is leaking underground between the curb stop and the home

inference.explanation: Meter movement with everything off, stopping at the curb stop, no indoor water, and peak noise midway along the service under the lawn localize an underground service leak. A running toilet would show indoors and would not peak midway under the lawn, and a main leak would not stop when the curb stop closes.

nextClue.prompt: Which next check best confirms the explanation and guides the fix?

options.label: Replace the meter and recheck the next bill
Replace all toilet fill valves in the home
Excavate at the peak noise point on the service and repair the line, then confirm the meter is still with fixtures off

nextClue.explanation: Excavation at the traced point confirms the service leak location and allows the repair that the meter test then verifies.

clueText.nc-a: The meter passed an accuracy check and the curb stop test already isolates the service.
clueText.nc-b: No toilet was running on inspection and indoor causes would not peak under the lawn.
clueText.nc-c: A split in the service is found at the noise peak, and after repair the meter is still with fixtures off.

tasks.prompt: Pressure in a small zone in British Columbia sags slowly each night and a pump runs longer to refill the tank, with no change in customer demand.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional zone with tank level and pump run logging. Demand records are stable.

evidence.label: Tank level falls faster overnight than last year, while overnight customer demand is unchanged in meter records.
Total pumped volume is up 15 percent with no new customers.
Daytime pressures are normal and no surface water is seen anywhere in the zone.
Step testing at night, closing zone sections one at a time, shows the loss stops when one older section is isolated.
Acoustic survey of that section finds a strong noise at a creek crossing main.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by all of the observations?

options.label: A leak in the older section at the creek crossing is losing water continuously, hidden by the creek
Customer demand has grown secretly by 15 percent
The tank level sensor is drifting and the pumps are overfilling
The pump is losing capacity and running longer for that reason

inference.explanation: Volume is up with no demand growth, step testing isolates the loss to one section, and acoustics peak at the creek crossing where leaked water would be hidden. A sensor drift would not raise real pumped volume, and a weakening pump would not be isolated by section step testing.

nextClue.prompt: Which next check best confirms the explanation and guides the fix?

options.label: Excavate or expose the creek crossing main at the acoustic peak and repair the leak, then compare overnight tank fall
Replace the tank level sensor
Add a larger pump to keep up with demand

nextClue.explanation: Exposing the crossing confirms the hidden leak, and the overnight tank fall comparison verifies the repair.

clueText.nc-a: A leaking joint is found at the crossing, and overnight tank fall returns to last year rate after repair.
clueText.nc-b: Pumped volume is metered real water, not a level sensor artefact.
clueText.nc-c: A larger pump would mask a continuous leak and waste treated water.

tasks.prompt: Ice builds up thickly over one spot on a gravel road in a northern Manitoba community all winter, while the rest of the road stays bare.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional community with mains buried below frost depth under gravel roads. Winter observations are recorded.

evidence.label: The ice mound grows steadily even during a two week extreme cold period with no melt weather.
Water sampled from the ice edge, melted, shows chlorine residual.
The mound sits directly over the water main alignment at a creek crossing dip in the road.
No surface water source or ditch flow reaches that spot in winter.
In spring, excavation finds the main joint below the mound leaking, and the mound does not return the next winter after repair.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by all of the observations?

options.label: Snow clearing is piling extra snow that hardens at that spot
A main leak is feeding water that freezes layer by layer into the ice mound over the main
Road drainage is ponding and freezing at a low spot
A natural spring is freezing at the road surface

inference.explanation: Chlorinated meltwater, steady growth with no melt weather, position over the main, and no return after the joint repair together prove a leak source. Drainage or spring water would not carry chlorine residual, and piled snow would not grow during a no melt cold period.

nextClue.prompt: Which next check best confirms the explanation and guides the fix?

options.label: Reroute road drainage to the spot
Plan a controlled spring excavation at the mound location with the leak repair crew and materials ready
Spread extra gravel over the mound each winter

nextClue.explanation: Spring excavation at the recorded mound location is the planned confirmation, since winter digging in frozen ground is avoided where pressure allows.

clueText.nc-a: No ditch flow reaches the spot in winter, so drainage is not the source.
clueText.nc-b: Excavation finds the leaking joint under the mound, and the road stays bare the following winter.
clueText.nc-c: Gravel would bury the symptom while treated water keeps leaking.

tasks.prompt: A school in Alberta receives a very high water bill for the summer term, though the school was closed and empty for most of it.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional school with a metered service and an irrigation system. Billing and site records are available.

evidence.label: Meter readings taken monthly by the utility show steady use all summer, including at night.
Site inspection finds a toilet block with several cisterns refilling continuously due to worn valves.
No irrigation ran that summer, as the system was drained for field work.
When the toilet block supply is isolated for a weekend trial, meter movement stops completely.
Neighbouring buildings on the same main have normal bills.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by all of the observations?

options.label: A main leak in front of the school is passing through the meter
Students were using the school all summer without records
Continuously refilling toilet cisterns in the closed school used the metered water all summer
The school meter over registered all summer

inference.explanation: Steady metered use in an empty building, worn cistern valves found on inspection, and complete stoppage when that block is isolated prove the indoor continuous use. A main leak in front of the school would not pass through its meter, and the meter stops correctly in the isolation trial.

nextClue.prompt: Which next check best confirms the explanation and guides the fix?

options.label: Replace the school meter
Excavate the main in front of the school
Repair the cistern valves and compare the next month metered use with the building occupied

nextClue.explanation: Valve repair followed by a normal occupied month comparison verifies the fix in billing terms.

clueText.nc-a: The meter stops and starts correctly in the isolation trial, so it is registering real flow.
clueText.nc-b: Main water loss would not register on the school meter.
clueText.nc-c: Metered use falls to a normal occupied level after the cistern repairs.

tasks.prompt: Zone flow records in Saskatchewan show a sudden step up in demand that has stayed exactly level, day and night, for ten days since a storm.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional zone with inlet flow logging. Storm and repair records are available.

evidence.label: Zone inflow rose by a steady amount within an hour of the storm and has not varied with time of day since.
Customer demand before the storm followed a normal day and night pattern.
No new customers or construction connections were made that week.
Night step testing isolates the extra flow to a section along a creek that flooded during the storm.
Listening in that section finds leak noise at a main joint near the creek bank.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by all of the observations?

options.label: A new customer began using a perfectly constant flow after the storm
The inlet meter was damaged by the storm and reads high
Residents all changed their habits after the storm
Storm flooding damaged a main joint by the creek, creating a constant leak that adds a flat flow day and night

inference.explanation: A flat, unvarying increase starting with the storm, isolated by step testing to the flooded creek section with leak noise at a joint, is a constant leak. Customer use varies by time of day, and a damaged meter would not be isolated to one section by step testing.

nextClue.prompt: Which next check best confirms the explanation and guides the fix?

options.label: Excavate the noisy joint by the creek and repair it, then confirm zone inflow returns to its old pattern
Replace the zone inlet meter
Wait a month to see if the new demand pattern settles

nextClue.explanation: Excavation at the step tested, noisy joint is the direct confirmation and repair.

clueText.nc-a: A joint displaced by flood scour is found leaking, and zone flow returns to its normal pattern after repair.
clueText.nc-b: Step testing isolated real flow to one section, so the inlet meter is reading real water.
clueText.nc-c: A constant leak will not settle, and step testing already located it.

tasks.prompt: Repeated pavement failures and sinkholes appear over one block of main in a British Columbia town, each repaired, each returning within a year.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional block with older main in sandy soil. Repair history is mapped.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by all of the observations?

options.label: A long running small leak is washing bedding fines away, creating voids that collapse as recurring sinkholes
The road builder used poor fill that settles every year
Storm sewers are washing out the road base from below
Tree roots are lifting and cracking the pavement

inference.explanation: Damp excavations in dry weather, chlorinated pooled water, washed out bedding around the main, and persistent leak noise along the block point to a chronic small leak eroding support. Poor road fill would not produce chlorinated water or leak noise, and storm sewers would not dampen the main trench in dry weather.

nextClue.prompt: Which next check best confirms the explanation and guides the fix?

options.label: Replace the road surface with thicker asphalt
Excavate the noisiest corroded section, repair the leak, and reinstate with compacted bedding, then monitor the block
Keep patching each sinkhole as it appears

nextClue.explanation: Repairing the leak and restoring bedding addresses both the water loss and the void formation, and monitoring verifies the sinkholes stop.

clueText.nc-a: Thicker asphalt does not stop water eroding the bedding below.
clueText.nc-b: A corroded leaking section is replaced, and no new sinkhole appears in the block over the next two years.
clueText.nc-c: Patching alone has already failed repeatedly because the leak keeps washing out bedding.

tasks.prompt: A homeowner in Manitoba finds the water meter spinning in the morning though the house was empty overnight, and a damp area appears by the foundation.

The damp foundation area is on the side where the service enters the home.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by all of the observations?

The service line is leaking just outside the foundation, before the home main valve
A toilet is running silently all night
The meter is faulty and spins without flow

inference.explanation: Flow stops only at the home main valve, no fixture is running, and saturated chlorinated soil sits at the service entry. That places a service leak just outside the foundation. A toilet would stop at its fixture valve, a faulty meter would not saturate soil with chlorinated water, and a city main leak would not stop at the home valve.

nextClue.prompt: Which next check best confirms the explanation and guides the fix?

options.label: Replace the meter
Replace all toilets in the home
Excavate at the foundation service entry and repair the service, then confirm the meter is still overnight

clueText.nc-a: The meter correctly stops at the home valve, so it is measuring real flow.
clueText.nc-b: All fixtures were inspected and isolated with no change in flow.
clueText.nc-c: A cracked service fitting is found at the entry, and after repair the meter is still overnight and the soil dries.

tasks.prompt: Minimum night flow in a small town in Alberta has crept up slowly over two years, with no sudden step and no new development.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional town with inlet logging over several years. Growth records show no new connections.

evidence.label: Night flow is up 30 percent over two years in a slow, steady creep.
Daytime demand is flat over the same period and population is unchanged.
Several small wet areas and valve boxes with standing water have been noted across town in the same period.
Acoustic survey finds many faint leak noises rather than one strong noise.
A program repairing the first six small service and joint leaks found drops night flow partway back toward the old level.

inference.prompt: Which explanation is best supported by all of the observations?

options.label: Residents are slowly using more water at night each year
The inlet meter is drifting upward slowly
Many small leaks have developed across the ageing system and together they are raising the night flow
One large hidden leak is responsible for the whole increase

inference.explanation: A slow creep, flat daytime demand, many faint noises and wet spots, and a partial night flow recovery from repairing six small leaks all indicate distributed small leakage. One large leak would give a stronger single noise and a step change, and a drifting meter would not respond to leak repairs.

nextClue.prompt: Which next check best confirms the explanation and guides the fix?

options.label: Continue the acoustic survey and small leak repair program and trend night flow after each repair batch
Excavate the town largest main looking for one big leak
Replace the inlet meter

nextClue.explanation: Continuing the program that is already measurably reducing night flow is the evidence based check and fix.

clueText.nc-a: Night flow continues to fall after each repair batch, confirming distributed small leaks were the cause.
clueText.nc-b: Survey found many faint noises, not one large leak location.
clueText.nc-c: Meter checks against a test meter show it reads accurately.

tasks.prompt: During a dry summer, a farmer in rural Saskatchewan reports a spring like flow in a ditch beside a supply main that has run all season.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional rural supply main crossing farmland. Ditch flow observations are recorded.

evidence.label: The ditch flow runs steadily through the driest weeks when natural ditch flow in the area has stopped.
Water in the ditch tests positive for chlorine residual.
The flow emerges from the bank directly above the buried supply main alignment.

A drainage tile is discharging groundwater at that point
The supply main is leaking and its water is surfacing through the ditch bank

inference.explanation: Chlorinated ditch water in a drought, emerging over the main alignment, and stopping when the section is isolated prove a main leak. Spring, irrigation, and tile water would not carry chlorine residual or stop with main isolation.

nextClue.prompt: Which next check best confirms the explanation and guides the fix?

options.label: Ask the farmer to fill the ditch section with soil
Excavate at the emergence point over the main and repair the leak, then confirm the ditch dries
Monitor the spring for a year before acting

nextClue.explanation: Excavation at the emergence point is the direct repair location confirmed by the isolation trial.

clueText.nc-a: Filling the ditch would hide the leak while treated water keeps escaping.
clueText.nc-b: A leaking coupling is found under the emergence point, and the ditch dries after repair.
clueText.nc-c: The isolation trial already proved the water comes from the main.

tasks.prompt: A pressure logger in a British Columbia zone records a brief pressure dip and recovery every few hours, day and night, that no customer demand explains.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional zone with a large commercial property at its edge. Logger and site records are available.

evidence.label: Each dip lasts about ten minutes and repeats at regular intervals around the clock.
A large property in the zone has an irrigation and process tank that refills through a float valve that has begun to slam open and shut.
When the property supply is isolated for a day in a trial, the dips disappear from the logger.
Customer demand in the zone is otherwise smooth and does not show the interval pattern.

A leak is opening and closing on a cycle in the zone

The logger battery is failing and creating false dips

inference.explanation: Dips at regular intervals around the clock, a float valve found slamming on the one large property, and a clean logger record during the isolation trial tie the pattern to that property refill behaviour. A leak would not cycle this regularly, utility pumps do not match the timing, and a failing logger would not be cured by isolating a property.

nextClue.prompt: Which next check best confirms the explanation and guides the fix?

options.label: Begin a leak survey of the whole zone
Replace the zone pump controls
Repair or replace the property float valve and log zone pressure for the following week
